name: Macrobiotic diet

lead: The macrobiotic diet centres on whole grains, especially brown rice, with vegetables, beans and sea vegetables, little or no animal food, and avoidance of refined sugar and processed items. It draws on Zen Buddhist ideas and the yin-yang idea that foods should be balanced.[1]

Followers describe benefits in energy, digestion and appearance through a clean, plant-based, low-fat diet. Research has examined it mainly in medical settings: a Mediterranean-macrobiotic hybrid was tested in a trial of 1,542 breast-cancer patients, and a macrobiotic Ma-Pi 2 diet has been studied in diabetes and reactive hypoglycemia.[2][3]

paras: A typical pattern is about 50 to 60 percent whole grains, 20 to 30 percent vegetables, and 5 to 10 percent beans and sea vegetables, with seasonal local food, small amounts of white fish and fruit, and some nightshades avoided.[1] George Ohsawa described ten stages of increasing restriction.[1]

Strict versions have been linked to malnutrition and deaths, and to B12 deficiency, iron-deficiency anemia and scurvy, with children especially vulnerable.[1][4][5] Medical bodies advise against relying on it to treat cancer.[1]

angle.text: Followers adopt it for a lean frame, clear skin and vitality from unrefined plant food. Appearance outcomes have not been measured in trials.

lead: The macrobiotic diet is a plant-centred eating philosophy that emphasises whole grains, vegetables, beans and sea vegetables, minimal animal products and no refined sugar. Followers cite lean physiques, clear skin and steady energy as outcomes of eating this way.[1]

It was proposed by Japanese physician Sagen Ishizuka, popularised by George Ohsawa in the 1930s, and brought to the United States by his student Michio Kushi, who taught from Cambridge, Massachusetts and founded the Kushi Institute.[1][2] Its yin-yang framework classes foods as expansive or contractive and aims for balance, with a target ratio of 5 to 1 reached via ten stages.[1]

In the 1960s the strictest form was promoted as a cure for cancer and other diseases; reviews and cancer organisations report no high-quality clinical evidence for this, and medical authorities have warned of nutritional harm.[1][3]
infobox: Brown rice, vegetables, beans, sea vegetables

paras: The pattern is based on whole grains with cooked vegetables and sea vegetables, local seasonal food and moderation. Spinach, beets, avocado and nightshades are avoided or limited, and fish and fruit are used sparingly.[1]

The diet has roots in Sagen Ishizuka's theories, was popularised by Ohsawa in the 1930s, and Ohsawa's Zen Macrobiotics appeared in 1965.[1] Kushi expanded it in the 1970s with the East West Journal and the Kushi Institute, which closed in 2017.[1] Grokipedia adds that Kushi co-founded Erewhon Natural Foods in Boston.[2]

The 1960s Zen macrobiotic diet claimed to cure cancer, epilepsy and infectious diseases, and Kushi later mixed in ideas such as astrology.[1] Forum users on T Nation relay stories of people recovering from cancer through macrobiotics.[4]

A 2024 randomised trial of a macro-Mediterranean diet in 1,542 breast-cancer patients tested recurrence outcomes.[5] The Ma-Pi 2 macrobiotic diet has been studied in a randomised crossover trial for reactive hypoglycemia.[6] A systematic review of diets for type 2 diabetes included macrobiotic diets.[7] The American Cancer Society reports no peer-reviewed evidence of benefit against cancer.[1]

Reviews note that restrictive vegetarian diets such as macrobiotic are associated with more widespread iron-deficiency anemia.[8] Macrobiotic infants have shown iron deficiency and impaired development.[9] In 1965 a young follower died of malnutrition, in 1966 a grand jury called the diet a public health hazard, and in 1971 the AMA council warned of great danger.[1]

The DIANA-5 randomised trial examined a diet based on Mediterranean and macrobiotic traditions for breast cancer recurrence in 1,542 patients.[5] A randomised crossover trial tested the Ma-Pi 2 macrobiotic diet in reactive hypoglycemia.[6] A 2019 systematic review of randomised trials examined macrobiotic and other diets in type 2 diabetes.[7] No trial has measured appearance outcomes.
